questions.question: Two Azure VNets are in the SAME REGION. Workloads in VNet-A need LOW-LATENCY (≤ 1 ms), high-bandwidth PRIVATE connectivity to a shared database in VNet-B. The link must use the Microsoft backbone, NOT IPsec encapsulation. Operating overhead must be minimal. Which connectivity option fits all three constraints?
options: Site-to-site VPN tunnel — IPsec overhead and gateway latency, opposite of the low-latency requirement
VNet peering in the same region — direct on-backbone routing, sub-millisecond latency, no gateway in the path
VPN Gateway with BGP — IPsec + gateway hop adds latency and cost; not the right fit for same-region
Azure Virtual WAN hub — designed for global multi-region transit, overkill and adds hub-hop latency
questions.explanation: Same-region VNet peering is the canonical low-latency, high-bandwidth private connection — traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone with no gateway between VNets. VPN/ExpressRoute add a gateway hop. Virtual WAN is for global transit. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked VPN-GW-with-BGP as the same-region low-latency answer) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A VM has both a SUBNET NSG and a NIC NSG attached. An INBOUND packet to port 443 arrives at the VM. In what order are the two NSGs evaluated for the inbound direction?
options: NIC NSG first then subnet NSG — that is the OUTBOUND order, not inbound
Subnet NSG first then NIC NSG — the documented INBOUND evaluation order
Most specific NSG (NIC) is evaluated and the other ignored — both are always evaluated
Both NSGs in parallel, most permissive wins — both must allow; either deny blocks
questions.explanation: Inbound: Subnet NSG → NIC NSG. Outbound: NIC NSG → Subnet NSG. Both must allow; either deny drops the packet. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index for the inbound direction — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A team needs browser-based, SSH/RDP access to Azure VMs WITHOUT (a) opening port 22/3389 to the internet, (b) deploying or operating any additional VMs (jump-boxes), and (c) installing client software. Which Azure service meets all three?
options: Deploy a jump-box VM with public IP and RDP open — violates (a) open port and (b) extra VM
Enable Just-in-Time VM access via Defender for Cloud — still requires public RDP/SSH listeners and the user's client
Azure Bastion — managed PaaS service that brokers browser-based RDP/SSH over TLS from the portal, no public 3389/22, no jump-box
NSG rule allowing RDP from the corporate IP range — still exposes RDP publicly, just narrower
questions.explanation: Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS bastion host: the user opens the VM in the Azure portal, Bastion proxies RDP/SSH through TLS from the browser, ports 22/3389 are NEVER public, and no jump-box is required. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked jump-box deployment, which violates the requirements) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: Two Windows VMs hosting a web tier in a single region need to meet Microsoft's 99.95% VM SLA. The SLA requires the two VMs be deployed in a configuration that protects against planned maintenance + unplanned hardware failures within the region. Which configuration is the MINIMUM that meets 99.95%?
options: Deploy both VMs into a single Availability Zone — 99.95% SLA needs DIFFERENT zones
Deploy both VMs into an Availability Set (different fault and update domains) — the documented configuration for 99.95% within one region
Deploy both VMs into two different regions fronted by Traffic Manager — exceeds the SLA (99.99%+) but is far more than the minimum
Deploy both VMs on Premium SSD disks — disk SLA, not the VM SLA
questions.explanation: Two or more VMs in an Availability Set across distinct fault + update domains gives the 99.95% VM SLA. Availability Zones give 99.99% (one VM per zone, ≥2 zones). Two-region + TM is multi-region DR. The QUESTION asks the MINIMUM for 99.95%, which is Availability Set. NOTE: prior version marked two-region (overkill) as the minimum — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A latency-sensitive workload needs (a) consistent sub-millisecond disk latency, (b) up to 160 000 IOPS and 4 000 MB/s throughput, (c) the ability to ADJUST IOPS and throughput AT RUNTIME WITHOUT restarting the VM or detaching the disk. Which Azure managed disk SKU supports ALL three?
options: Premium SSD v2 — supports independent IOPS/throughput dimensions and sub-ms latency, very close fit
Standard SSD — performance class too low for sub-ms / 160k IOPS
Ultra Disk — sub-ms latency, up to 160k IOPS / 4 GB/s, IOPS + throughput tunable AT RUNTIME without VM restart
Premium SSD v1 — IOPS is FIXED by disk size tier (P1, P10, P30...); cannot tune at runtime independently
questions.explanation: Ultra Disk is the original SKU supporting fully independent and online-adjustable IOPS + throughput, sub-ms latency, and the highest performance ceiling. Premium SSD v2 is similar and is the modern competitor, but Premium SSD v1 has fixed IOPS per size tier and cannot be tuned online. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked Premium SSD v1 as the online-tunable IOPS SKU) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An organisation runs on-prem Active Directory and wants employees to sign in to Microsoft 365 with their on-prem credentials, with PASSWORD VALIDATION HAPPENING AGAINST THE ON-PREM AD DOMAIN CONTROLLER (no password hashes synced to Azure AD). Which Azure AD Connect sign-in method fits this constraint?
options: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) — Azure AD validates against the SYNCED HASH, not against the on-prem DC
Pass-through Authentication (PTA) — Azure AD Connect agent forwards the auth attempt to an on-prem DC for validation; no hashes stored in Azure AD
Federation with AD FS — also validates on-prem but requires running AD FS farm; PTA is the lightweight alternative
Azure AD Connect cloud sync only — sync agent, but PHS is the actual sign-in method behind cloud sync
questions.explanation: Pass-through Authentication (PTA) validates passwords directly against on-premises AD in real time without storing any password hash in Azure AD. An on-premises agent receives the authentication request from Azure AD, validates it locally, and returns the result. This satisfies the requirement that password hashes never leave the corporate network. PHS stores a hash of the hash in Azure AD, which fails the requirement. AD FS also keeps authentication on-premises but requires additional infrastructure.

questions.question: An app subnet must force ALL outbound internet-bound traffic through a third-party firewall NVA at 10.0.1.4 before it leaves Azure. The NVA must intercept and inspect, then forward out. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Outbound NSG deny `0.0.0.0/0` on the subnet — silently drops egress, doesn't route via NVA
User-Defined Route (UDR) for `0.0.0.0/0` with next hop `Virtual Appliance` 10.0.1.4 associated to the subnet — forces traffic through the NVA
Enable IP forwarding only on the VM NICs — flag is needed ON THE NVA, but alone doesn't route the app subnet's egress through it
VNet peering with gateway transit — connectivity feature, not an egress-forcing route
questions.explanation: A User Defined Route (UDR) in a route table overrides Azure's default system routes. Setting a route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop type 'Virtual Appliance' and next hop IP 10.0.1.4 forces all internet-bound traffic through the NVA. The route table must be associated with the application subnet. IP forwarding must be enabled on the NVA's NIC (not the application VMs). NSG rules filter traffic but cannot redirect it to another device.

questions.question: An app behind a STANDARD-tier Application Gateway is being SQL-injected. The team wants to block injection patterns at the load-balancer tier (no app-code change). The Standard SKU does NOT include WAF. Which upgrade enables a managed OWASP rule set in front of the app?
options: Switch WAF policy mode from Detection to Prevention — requires the WAF SKU first, which Standard does not have
Upgrade the Application Gateway SKU from Standard_v2 to WAF_v2 — adds OWASP CRS managed rules, switchable to Prevention mode
Enable Azure DDoS Network Protection — L3/L4 protection, not application-layer SQLi
Add NSG rules blocking source IPs — reactive, not preventive at the WAF layer
questions.explanation: Azure Application Gateway WAF operates in two modes: Detection (logs threats but does not block) and Prevention (actively blocks requests matching OWASP rules, including SQL injection). Switching to Prevention mode causes the WAF to block and log requests matching managed rule sets like OWASP 3.2. The WAF_v2 SKU already supports WAF policies; upgrading SKU is not the issue. DDoS Standard protects against volumetric attacks, not application-layer injection. NSG rules cannot inspect HTTP payload content.

questions.question: An admin needs a SINGLE service that ingests Azure VM perf counters, Azure Activity Log entries, AKS container logs, and Application Insights traces, then lets them join across those tables with KQL queries. Which Azure component fits?
options: Azure Monitor Metrics Explorer — chart metrics, no KQL log-join across diverse sources
Azure Application Insights component — app-only telemetry, narrower scope, not the multi-service unified log store
Azure Log Analytics workspace — the unified log store for multiple Azure services, queried with KQL
Azure Event Hubs namespace — high-throughput ingestion, not a queryable log store
questions.explanation: Log Analytics workspaces are the unified KQL-queryable log store. Activity Log, VM diagnostic logs, AKS container logs, Application Insights, and resource logs can all be routed to a single workspace. Metrics Explorer is metrics-only; App Insights is app-only telemetry; Event Hubs is a pipeline, not a queryable store. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked Application Insights as the multi-service log store) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A company stores 7-year compliance archives in Azure Blob Storage. Access frequency is near zero (rare audit retrieval, hours-of-restore latency is acceptable). MINIMUM storage cost is the priority. Which blob access tier should they use?
options: Hot — frequent access pricing, highest storage cost, lowest retrieval cost
Cool — infrequent access (≥30 days), cheaper than hot, more expensive than cold/archive
Cold — rare access (≥90 days), cheaper than cool, more expensive than archive
Archive — offline tier with rehydration delay (hours), CHEAPEST storage cost, ideal for 7-year compliance retention rarely retrieved
questions.explanation: Archive is the cheapest blob storage tier and is designed precisely for compliance / legal-hold data that is rarely retrieved and tolerates hours of rehydration latency. Cold is for rare access but still online; Cool for monthly access; Hot for frequent. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked Cold as cheapest; Archive is) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: VMs in a VNet must access an Azure Storage account so that (a) traffic travels via the Azure backbone with a PRIVATE IP, (b) the storage account is reachable on a private DNS name from within the VNet, and (c) public storage endpoints can be blocked entirely. Which feature satisfies all three?
options: Storage Service Endpoint with VNet rule — keeps traffic on backbone but the storage account still has a public DNS, no private IP into the VNet
Private Endpoint for the storage account — gives the storage account a private NIC in the VNet with a private IP and private-DNS name; public endpoint can be disabled
Storage firewall with `trusted Azure services` exception — exception only for select Microsoft services, not the VM scenario
VPN Gateway with forced tunneling — VPN feature, irrelevant to PaaS-storage private access
questions.explanation: A Private Endpoint creates a private IP address inside your VNet that maps to the storage account. DNS resolves the storage account FQDN to this private IP, so all traffic (including from on-premises via ExpressRoute) stays on private networks. A Service Endpoint keeps traffic on the Azure backbone but the storage account still has a public endpoint and the private IP is not accessible from on-premises without additional DNS configuration. Private Endpoints support on-premises access natively when DNS is configured correctly.

questions.question: Regulation requires Azure VM disks to be encrypted at TWO LAYERS: (a) at the storage platform layer, and (b) inside the guest OS itself. Which combination meets both layers?
options: Server-Side Encryption (SSE) with platform-managed keys ALONE — covers storage layer only, no OS-layer encryption
Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) using BitLocker / dm-crypt ALONE — covers OS layer only, no separate storage-layer key
SSE-with-PMK PLUS Azure Disk Encryption — two distinct layers: SSE at the storage platform + ADE inside the guest OS
A customer-managed storage account with manual key-based encryption — not the documented two-layer combo
questions.explanation: SSE protects the disk at the Azure storage platform; ADE protects the OS-resident filesystem with BitLocker (Windows) or dm-crypt (Linux). Both layers together gives defence-in-depth. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An organization needs to ensure that all Windows VMs in Azure automatically have a specific set of Windows features installed and services running. When a VM drifts from this configuration, it should be automatically corrected. Which service provides this capability?
options: Azure Policy with the DeployIfNotExists effect
Azure Automation Desired State Configuration (DSC)
Azure Update Manager maintenance configurations
Custom Script Extension assigned to each VM
questions.explanation: Azure Automation DSC is a pull-based configuration management service. You define the desired state (installed features, running services, registry settings) in a PowerShell DSC configuration, publish it to an Automation account, and register VMs as nodes. Nodes check in every 15–30 minutes, compare their current state to the desired state, and automatically correct any drift. Azure Policy can deploy configurations but does not provide the continuous compliance loop. Custom Script Extension runs once at deployment and does not monitor or correct drift.

questions.question: A compliance team needs to apply 30 related Azure Policy definitions (CIS benchmark) to a management group AS A SINGLE GROUPED UNIT — one assignment, one set of parameters, one compliance report. Re-assigning the 30 individually means 30 assignments to maintain. Which feature provides 'package of definitions' semantics?
options: Assign each of the 30 definitions individually to the management group — defeats the single-unit grouped-set requirement
Azure Policy Initiative (Policy Set definition) — groups multiple definitions and is assigned + reported as a single set/unit
Custom policy definition with all 30 rules in JSON — combines definitions into one set technically but is brittle, not the management-group unit pattern
Azure Blueprints — bundles definitions + ARM templates + RBAC as a unit; broader than a Policy Set/Initiative grouping (retired July 2026)
questions.explanation: An Azure Policy initiative (also called a policy set) groups multiple policy definitions into a single assignable unit. This allows assigning all 30 CIS controls with one initiative assignment and tracking combined compliance as a single percentage score. Built-in initiatives include CIS, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001. Azure Blueprints can include policy assignments as artifacts but are not required for this scenario. Embedding 30 rules into a single policy definition is not supported by the policy schema.

questions.question: An admin needs a single backup target supporting (a) Azure VM backup, (b) SQL Server in Azure VM backup, (c) on-prem Windows file servers via the MARS agent. Which Azure resource is the target for all three?
options: Backup vault (newer) — covers Postgres, Disks, Blobs, Files; does NOT cover VM/MARS today
Recovery Services vault — canonical target for VM, SQL-in-VM, MARS, and ASR
Azure Storage account — Backup uses a vault, not raw storage account, as the control plane
Site Recovery vault — same resource type as Recovery Services but configured for replication, not backup workloads
questions.explanation: Recovery Services vault is the long-standing target for Azure VM, SQL-in-VM, MARS-agent, and ASR replication. Newer Backup vault SKU does not yet cover MARS/VM at parity. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A Conditional Access policy is configured to require MFA when users sign in from outside the corporate network. A user successfully completes MFA from home. The next day, the same user signs in from the corporate office (a Named Location marked as trusted). What happens?
options: The user is challenged for MFA on this sign-in regardless of network location
The policy excludes the trusted Named Location, so MFA is not triggered
The user must re-authenticate with MFA because a fresh session is starting
Conditional Access is bypassed because the user completed MFA within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Conditional Access policies evaluate signals at sign-in time. If the Named Location (corporate office IP range) is marked as trusted and the policy condition requires MFA only when signing in from outside trusted locations, the policy's condition is not met for corporate office sign-ins, so MFA is not triggered. This is the intended behavior: Named Locations let organizations define trusted network ranges that are excluded from certain CA requirements, reducing friction for on-site employees.

questions.question: An autoscale rule must launch 50 new D4s_v3 VMs (4 vCPUs each) in East US within minutes. The subscription's regional compute-quota for the new D-series VMs in East US currently allows only 100 vCPUs. The deployment fails on the 26th new VM. What's the right fix?
options: Submit a new Azure quota-increase request for D-series vCPUs in East US (per-family per-region) — the new ceiling resolves the failure
Move the new VMs to a different Azure resource group — RGs do not have vCPU quota; same subscription limits apply
Switch to spot VMs for the new fleet — different priority but still bound by the new D-series vCPU quota in East US
Recreate the new VM scale set in a different Azure region — quota is per-region; if the new region also has 100 vCPU limit, identical failure
questions.explanation: Azure enforces per-region, per-VM-family vCPU quotas (soft limits). The default is often 20 vCPUs per family per region. To deploy 50 D4s_v3 VMs (200 vCPUs) you need to request a quota increase. This is done in the Azure Portal under Subscriptions > Usage + quotas, where you can submit a support request for a specific VM family in a specific region. Moving to a different resource group does not change the subscription-level quota. Creating a new subscription is a workaround, not a recommended practice.

questions.question: An organisation wants security administrators to hold Global Administrator only when actively needed, with: explicit activation request, just-in-time elevation, optional approval workflow, and full audit trail of every activation. Which Azure AD feature fits all four?
options: Azure AD Conditional Access session controls — gates EXISTING sessions, no JIT role activation
Azure RBAC time-bound assignments — gives the role for a time window, no activation workflow
Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) — JIT eligible activation, approval, MFA, time-bound, audit
Azure AD custom role definitions — defines permissions, no JIT/activation
questions.explanation: PIM makes a role ELIGIBLE rather than ACTIVE. Activation requires the user to request it; PIM enforces MFA, time-bound expiry, and logs every activation. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A team is choosing between Basic and Standard Load Balancer SKUs for a zone-redundant, multi-AZ deployment. They need: (a) frontends and backend pools that survive an AZ outage, (b) HA Ports for active/standby NVAs. Which statement about the SKUs is correct?
options: Standard SKU supports internal-only with zone-redundant frontends; Basic supports both — false, opposite
Standard SKU supports zone-redundant frontends and backends across AZs; Basic SKU is not zone-aware (no zone-redundant frontends)
Standard SKU requires VPN GW for zone-redundant failover; Basic does not — false, neither requires VPN GW for zone-redundant frontends
Standard SKU is capped at 100 backends; Basic supports unlimited zone-redundant backend frontends — false, Standard scales higher
questions.explanation: Standard Load Balancer is the production SKU: zone-redundant + zonal frontends, multi-AZ backend pools, HA Ports, secure-by-default (deny unless allowed), 1000-instance pools. Basic is the legacy SKU, no zone awareness, slated for retirement Sept 2025. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An admin accidentally deleted a critical RG. The team wants to prevent any future deletion of that RG without revoking any user's RBAC role and without writing custom policy. Which Azure feature is purpose-built for this?
options: A ReadOnly lock on the RG — prevents UPDATES too, which is more than needed and breaks ops
A CanNotDelete lock at the RG scope — blocks every delete (even by Owners), still allows reads + updates, no RBAC change
A ReadOnly lock on each resource individually — fragile, blocks legitimate updates
A deny assignment at the subscription level — used internally by Blueprints / Managed Apps, not the admin-facing protection feature
questions.explanation: Resource Manager locks live ABOVE RBAC. CanNotDelete blocks deletes for everyone (including Owners) until removed. ReadOnly is heavier (also blocks updates). Deny-assignments are an internal mechanism. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: VMs in a VNet must resolve internal hostnames like `appserver.internal.contoso.com` to private IPs WITHOUT operating any DNS server VM. The zone must be authoritative for `internal.contoso.com` and visible only inside linked VNets, with VMs auto-registering their A records. Which feature?
options: Azure-provided DNS only — provides the default resolver, not authoritative for a custom zone
Azure Private DNS zone with auto-registration enabled, linked to the VNet — managed PaaS, no VM to operate
Public Azure DNS zone — answers on the public internet, opposite of private
Windows Server DNS VM — works but requires an extra VM (excluded)
questions.explanation: Azure Private DNS zones provide DNS name resolution within VNets without needing a custom DNS server. Linking a private zone to a VNet with auto-registration enabled causes Azure to automatically create and update DNS records (A records with the VM's hostname and private IP) when VMs are created, updated, or deleted. Multiple VNets can be linked to the same private zone for cross-VNet name resolution. Azure-provided DNS uses a fixed suffix (*.internal.cloudapp.net) and cannot be customized to use your own domain.

questions.question: A team needs to run a SHORT-LIVED containerised data-processing job that completes in <10 minutes. Requirements: no cluster/infra to manage, per-second billing for the runtime, just submit the image and run. Which Azure service fits all three?
options: Azure Kubernetes Service — requires running node-pool VMs even when no jobs run; fails the no-infra requirement
Azure Container Instances (ACI) — serverless, per-second billing for runtime, no cluster
App Service Web App for Containers — long-running web hosting, not a short-lived job
Service Fabric — cluster-based, fails the no-infra requirement
questions.explanation: ACI is the serverless container runtime: submit an image, the container runs, billing is per second, no cluster ops. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An admin must stream Azure VM resource logs + platform metrics to BOTH (a) a 3rd-party SIEM via Event Hub in real time AND (b) an Azure Storage account for long-term archive. The mechanism is configured per-resource, natively. Which feature?
options: Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules — collects guest-OS data INTO the agent stream, not a multi-destination resource fan-out
Azure Diagnostic Settings — native per-resource fan-out to Log Analytics + Storage + Event Hub + partner SIEM destinations
Azure Automation runbook — automation, not a real-time diagnostic stream
Logic App triggered by an alert — alert-driven action, not a diagnostic-stream
questions.explanation: Diagnostic Settings on a resource route platform logs + metrics natively to any combination of Log Analytics, Storage, Event Hub (for SIEM ingestion), and partner solutions. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: Employees of a partner organisation (different Azure AD tenant) need to access internal SharePoint and Azure resources in our tenant, signing in with their home tenant credentials. We don't want local accounts and we don't want to merge tenants. Which Azure AD feature?
options: Azure AD B2C — designed for external customer / consumer identity, not partner-tenant collaboration
Azure AD B2B Collaboration with Guest user accounts — partner users sign in with their home tenant credentials and are invited as Guests in our tenant
Azure AD Connect cloud sync — syncs on-prem AD, not cross-tenant collaboration
Create local accounts for partner users — exactly what the requirement forbids
questions.explanation: B2B Collaboration invites users from another tenant (or any IdP) as Guests in our tenant; they auth at home, are authorised here. B2C is a separate product for consumer identity. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A VM scale set autoscale-in is triggered. ONE instance is mid-way through a 3-hour batch job and must NOT be terminated. Other instances must remain eligible to scale-in. Which feature protects only that single instance?
options: Switch the whole VMSS to manual scaling — overly broad; freezes all scaling
Apply ProtectFromScaleIn Instance Protection to the specific instance — VMSS skips it during scale-in while continuing to manage others
Enable termination notifications with a delay — only delays termination, doesn't prevent it
Pin a static private IP — IP reservation doesn't affect scale-in selection
questions.explanation: Instance Protection has two flags: ProtectFromScaleIn (autoscale-in skips it) and ProtectFromScaleSetActions (skips VMSS-wide ops). Set per-instance. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: After deploying a Windows VM from an Azure Marketplace image, an administrator needs to automatically join it to a domain and install a custom application. The VM must not have a public IP. Which approach accomplishes this without requiring SSH/RDP access?
options: RDP into the VM after deployment and run the configuration scripts manually
Use Azure Bastion to SSH or RDP into the VM after deployment completes
Add the Custom Script Extension and Domain Join Extension to the template
Create a Scheduled Task inside the VM image that runs on the first boot
questions.explanation: Azure VM Extensions are lightweight components that run post-deployment configuration on VMs. The Custom Script Extension can download and execute PowerShell or Bash scripts to install software. The Domain Join Extension handles Active Directory domain join operations using stored credentials. Both extensions can be included in ARM templates, Bicep, or added after deployment via the Portal or CLI. They run in the VM's context without requiring any remote access (no public IP or open ports needed). Multiple extensions can run sequentially on a single VM.

questions.question: An ops team needs to schedule monthly OS-security patching on a fleet of Azure VMs (Windows + Linux) during a maintenance window every last Sunday 02:00-06:00. The chosen service must support recurring schedules, multi-VM scope (subscription / management group / tag selectors), and per-classification (Critical / Security) patch picking. Which service fits?
options: Azure Automation Update Management (classic) — earlier recurring-maintenance schedule tool, retired in favour of newer service
Azure Update Manager maintenance configurations — current recurring maintenance schedule with subscription/MG/tag scope
Hotpatch-enabled VMs auto-patching — Windows Server Azure Edition only, no admin-defined recurring maintenance schedule scope
Azure Policy with `audit` effect — audits patch state, no maintenance scheduling for recurring scope
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager uses maintenance configurations to define recurring schedules for patching. You can specify recurrence (monthly, last Sunday), start time, duration (2-hour window), and scope (specific VMs, resource groups, or subscriptions via Azure Policy). The maintenance configuration is associated with VMs, and Update Manager handles the orchestrated patching. Azure Automation Update Management is the legacy solution being replaced by Azure Update Manager. VM auto-patching uses Azure-defined windows, not customer-defined schedules. Azure Policy audit effects only report compliance, they do not patch VMs.

questions.question: A global SaaS app has backends in East US AND West Europe. Requirements: route users to the geographically closest HEALTHY backend; fail over instantly to the other region on backend failure; terminate TLS at the edge with WAF inspection; anycast public IP rather than per-region DNS. Which front-end best fits all four?
options: Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based at the resolver edge, no anycast IP, no edge TLS termination
Azure Front Door + WAF — anycast IP at the edge, edge TLS termination, latency-based edge routing, integrated edge WAF
Azure Load Balancer Standard — regional, no edge presence or WAF
Azure CDN Premium — caching-first edge, no edge WAF policy of the same shape
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global Layer 7 load balancer that combines: latency-based routing to the closest healthy origin, automatic health probing and failover, WAF policies (at the global entry point), DDoS protection, SSL offload, and CDN capabilities. Unlike Traffic Manager (which is DNS-based and does not process HTTP traffic), Front Door operates at the application layer and can inspect, modify, and route HTTP requests. This makes it the ideal single service for this scenario.

questions.question: A security audit asks WHO deleted a production VM yesterday at 14:47 UTC and FROM WHICH IP. The investigation must rely on a tenant-wide, immutable, default-on plane-of-record log. Which Azure log is the authoritative source?
options: Azure Activity Log — tenant-wide control-plane log of who/what/when/where for management operations, immutable, default-on; the right answer for this security audit
Azure VM Boot Diagnostics — captures boot images of the VM, no security audit trail of the deletion event
Azure Network Watcher Flow Logs — L4 traffic flows for security/network analytics, not control-plane CRUD audit
Azure Application Insights traces — application telemetry from inside the app, not Azure-RM control-plane security audit
questions.explanation: The Azure Activity Log records all subscription-level management plane operations, including resource creation, modification, and deletion. Each entry includes the caller (user principal name or service principal), timestamp, operation name, result (Succeeded/Failed), and resource details. Filtering by 'Delete VirtualMachines' operation in the target subscription will show the exact deletion event. The Activity Log is retained for 90 days by default but can be exported to Log Analytics or Storage for longer retention. Metrics track performance data, not control-plane operations.

questions.question: A high-performance computing (HPC) application requires shared file storage accessible by hundreds of Linux VMs simultaneously via NFS v4.1, with consistent sub-millisecond latency and throughput of over 1,000 MB/s. Which Azure storage service is designed for this workload?
options: Azure Files Premium shared SMB — managed but max throughput per share limits HPC shared workloads
Azure NetApp Files with NFS 4.1 protocol — shared low-latency high-throughput file storage built for HPC and EDA workloads
Azure Disk shared mode — block-level shared disk, no POSIX file semantics for shared HPC reads
Azure Blob shared NFS 3.0 — shared object-store NFS, optimised for read-heavy not low-latency shared HPC writes
questions.explanation: Azure NetApp Files is an enterprise NAS service powered by NetApp hardware designed for latency-sensitive, high-throughput workloads. The Ultra service level provides 128 MB/s of throughput per TiB of provisioned capacity and sub-millisecond latency. It natively supports NFS v3 and NFS v4.1 for Linux workloads. For an HPC application requiring 1,000 MB/s, a sufficiently provisioned Ultra-tier volume (approximately 8 TiB at 128 MB/s/TiB) would meet requirements. Azure Files Premium uses SMB 3.x primarily (NFS 4.1 is also supported but throughput is lower). Shared Ultra Disks are designed for clustered applications, not hundreds of simultaneous NFS clients.

questions.question: A CISO wants a SINGLE dashboard that surfaces (a) unpatched OS vulns per VM, (b) public-exposed storage accounts, (c) drift from CIS benchmarks, and (d) a numeric posture score that improves as recommendations are remediated. The score is the executive KPI. Which Azure feature is this?
options: Azure Monitor custom workbook — possible to build similar feature manually, lacks the named score + recommendations engine
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score and recommendations — the named feature providing both posture score and remediation recommendations
Azure Policy compliance dashboard — shows policy pass/fail recommendations, no numeric posture-score feature
Microsoft Sentinel workbook — threat-hunting feature, not a posture recommendations engine
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud (formerly Azure Security Center) provides Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM). The Secure Score is a percentage representing how many security recommendations have been implemented out of the total available. Each recommendation is prioritized by potential security impact. The free CSPM tier covers Azure resources; enhanced Defender plans (Defender for Servers, Storage, Containers, etc.) add threat detection and advanced vulnerability scanning. Azure Policy measures regulatory compliance but does not provide the security posture scoring that Defender for Cloud does.

questions.question: An administrator needs to automatically start all VMs tagged with 'Environment: Dev' every weekday morning at 7:00 AM and stop them at 7:00 PM to reduce costs. Which Azure service enables this scheduled automation?
options: Azure Logic Apps with a recurrence trigger
Azure Policy with DeployIfNotExists effect
Azure Automation runbook with a schedule
Azure DevOps pipeline with a cron trigger
questions.explanation: Azure Automation runbooks are PowerShell or Python scripts stored in an Automation account that can be triggered on a schedule. A runbook can query all VMs with a specific tag using the Azure PowerShell module and start or stop them using Start-AzVM and Stop-AzVM cmdlets. A schedule is attached to the runbook (e.g., weekdays at 7:00 AM for start, 7:00 PM for stop). The runbook runs in an Azure sandbox without requiring any VM access. Azure Logic Apps could also work but Automation runbooks are the more common and cost-effective choice for scheduled VM management.

questions.question: A user attempts to reset their own Azure AD password but receives an error stating the feature is not enabled. The administrator wants to allow users to reset their passwords independently without IT helpdesk involvement. Which feature must be configured?
options: Azure AD MFA registration policy enforcement
Azure AD Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR)
Azure AD Password Protection global banned list
Azure AD Identity Protection sign-in risk policy
questions.explanation: Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR) allows users to reset or unlock their own passwords without contacting the IT helpdesk. Administrators enable SSPR for all users or selected groups in Azure AD > Password reset. Users must register at least one authentication method (mobile app, phone, email, security questions). SSPR can be configured for cloud-only accounts or, with password writeback via Azure AD Connect, for on-premises hybrid accounts. Azure AD MFA registration enables MFA enrollment but does not enable password self-service.

questions.question: A Conditional Access policy must BLOCK legacy authentication protocols (IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH, MAPI) because they bypass MFA. The policy must apply to all users and all cloud apps. Which condition + control combination achieves this?
options: Condition: all cloud apps. Control: Require MFA — wrong; legacy clients can't satisfy MFA so they need BLOCK, not MFA
Condition: Client apps = Legacy authentication clients. Control: Block access
Condition: Sign-in risk = High. Control: Require MFA — risk-based, not legacy-protocol gating
Condition: Device platform = Unknown. Control: Block — too broad and not protocol-specific
questions.explanation: The 'Client apps' condition in Conditional Access can target specific authentication flows. Selecting 'Legacy authentication clients' (which covers Exchange ActiveSync and other older protocols that use basic authentication) and applying a 'Block access' control prevents any sign-in using those protocols. Simply requiring MFA for legacy auth would not help because legacy protocols cannot perform MFA challenges — they must be blocked outright. This is a critical security configuration as legacy authentication is a common attack vector for password spray attacks.

questions.question: Azure VMs in a subnet need to initiate outbound connections to the internet without being assigned individual public IP addresses. The solution must support a large number of concurrent connections and provide a static outbound IP for allowlisting by external services. Which Azure service should be deployed?
options: Azure Load Balancer Standard with outbound rules configured
Azure NAT Gateway attached to the application subnet
Azure Firewall deployed in the hub VNet for egress
Assign a dedicated public IP to each application VM NIC
questions.explanation: Azure NAT Gateway provides outbound-only internet connectivity for an entire subnet without requiring public IPs on individual VMs. It supports up to 64,512 SNAT ports per associated public IP address (and up to 16 public IPs per NAT Gateway, providing over 1 million ports). The public IP(s) associated with NAT Gateway are static and predictable, making them ideal for external allowlisting. NAT Gateway is the recommended solution for outbound-only internet access. Load Balancer outbound rules also work but NAT Gateway provides more SNAT ports and is simpler to configure for this purpose.

questions.question: An application's users are distributed globally. The company wants DNS-based routing that sends users in Europe to European backends and users in Asia to Asian backends. If a regional backend is unhealthy, traffic should automatically shift to the next healthy region. Which Azure Traffic Manager routing method achieves this?
options: Weighted routing
Performance routing
Priority routing
Geographic routing
questions.explanation: Geographic routing in Azure Traffic Manager maps user DNS queries to specific endpoints based on the geographic location of the DNS resolver. Users in Europe are routed to European endpoints; users in Asia to Asian endpoints. When combined with endpoint health probes, Traffic Manager can automatically exclude unhealthy endpoints, causing the next applicable geographic mapping to be used. Performance routing routes to the lowest-latency endpoint globally (not strictly by continent). Geographic routing is the correct choice when you need deterministic regional assignment regardless of latency.

questions.question: A company needs to resolve DNS names in an on-premises data center from Azure Private DNS zones, and also resolve on-premises DNS names from Azure VMs. A solution is needed that does not require deploying and managing custom DNS server VMs. Which Azure service provides inbound and outbound DNS forwarding for hybrid environments?
options: Azure DNS Private Resolver for hybrid forwarding scenarios
Azure Firewall with the DNS proxy feature enabled on it
Azure Private DNS zone with VNet links in both directions
Azure VPN Gateway with BGP and DNS relay configuration
questions.explanation: Azure DNS Private Resolver is a fully managed service that provides inbound DNS forwarding (on-premises resolvers can forward queries to Azure and receive answers from Private DNS zones) and outbound DNS forwarding (Azure VMs can forward queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS servers). This eliminates the need to deploy and manage custom DNS server VMs (such as Windows Server DNS or BIND) in Azure. Azure Firewall can proxy DNS but is primarily a network security appliance, not a dedicated DNS resolution service for hybrid scenarios.

questions.question: A VM scale set is configured with an autoscale rule to add 2 instances when average CPU exceeds 75% for 10 minutes. An administrator notices the scale set is adding and removing instances rapidly every few minutes, causing instability. What setting should be adjusted to reduce this behavior?
options: Increase the CPU threshold from 75% up to 95% for triggering
Increase the autoscale cooldown period between scaling actions
Disable the scale-in rule on the scale set to stop oscillation
Switch from CPU-based scaling rules to schedule-based scaling
questions.explanation: Autoscale cooldown is the wait time after a scaling action before another scaling action can occur. If the cooldown is too short (or the default 5 minutes is insufficient for the workload), new instances may come online, temporarily reduce CPU, trigger a scale-in, and then CPU spikes again causing rapid oscillation (known as flapping). Increasing the cooldown period gives newly added instances time to fully absorb load before the autoscale engine evaluates conditions again. Simply raising the CPU threshold may prevent scale-out from triggering when needed.

questions.question: A company wants to reduce compute costs for a non-critical batch processing workload that can tolerate interruptions. The workload runs for up to 6 hours and can be restarted from a checkpoint if evicted. Which VM pricing model minimizes cost for this scenario?
options: Reserved Virtual Machine Instances on a 1-year term
Azure Spot VMs with an eviction policy on the SKU
Azure Savings Plan for Compute commitment pricing
Pay-as-you-go pricing with VM auto-shutdown enabled
questions.explanation: Azure Spot VMs allow you to use Azure's unused compute capacity at significant discounts (up to 90% off pay-as-you-go pricing). Spot VMs can be evicted when Azure needs capacity back, so they are only suitable for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch processing with checkpointing. Reserved Instances provide discounts but require a 1-year or 3-year commitment and are not suitable for short batch jobs. Savings Plans reduce costs for consistent compute usage. Auto-shutdown helps limit costs but does not provide the deep discount of Spot pricing.

questions.question: A production VM and a latency-sensitive database VM must have the lowest possible network latency between them. The two VMs must be physically located as close together as possible on the underlying Azure hardware. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Deploy both VMs into the same Availability Set in-region
Deploy both VMs into the same Availability Zone in-region
Deploy both VMs into the same Proximity Placement Group
Deploy both VMs into the same resource group together
questions.explanation: A Proximity Placement Group (PPG) is a logical grouping that ensures VMs are placed physically close together on the same underlying host cluster, minimizing network latency between them. This is important for latency-sensitive applications like an application server and its paired database VM. Availability Sets and Availability Zones intentionally spread VMs across separate fault domains or separate buildings to improve availability, which increases physical distance and latency. A resource group is a logical management construct with no impact on physical placement.

questions.question: A Windows dev team needs to share config files and binaries across multiple Azure VMs via SMB 3.x, with Active-Directory-DS authentication (not just a storage-account key), and a fully managed service (no file-server VM to operate). Which storage service fits all three?
options: Azure Blob with NFS 3.0 — NFS authentication for Linux, no SMB/AD authentication for Windows
Azure Files (Standard or Premium) with AD-DS authentication — managed SMB 3.x file share with Kerberos authentication via on-prem AD-DS
Azure NetApp Files SMB 3.x with AD-DS authentication — also AD-DS authentication capable, premium-priced specialty service
Azure Shared Managed Disk — block storage with no SMB/file authentication concept at all
questions.explanation: Azure Files provides fully managed SMB file shares in the cloud. It supports SMB 3.x protocol, which is compatible with Windows VMs. Azure Files supports identity-based access control via on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) or Azure AD DS, allowing users and VMs to authenticate with their existing AD credentials. This replaces traditional Windows file servers. Azure NetApp Files also supports SMB but is enterprise NAS for high-performance workloads and is more expensive. Blob Storage's NFS 3.0 support is for Linux workloads only.

questions.question: An external partner application needs read access to a specific blob container in an Azure Storage account for 48 hours. The partner must not have permanent credentials or an Azure AD identity. Which mechanism provides time-limited, scoped access?
options: Share the storage account access key directly with the partner organization
Create a Shared Access Signature (SAS) token scoped to the container, 48-hour expiry
Create a guest user account in Azure AD and assign Storage Blob Data Reader role
Enable anonymous blob read access on the specific container for the partner
questions.explanation: A Shared Access Signature (SAS) token provides delegated, time-limited access to specific storage resources without sharing the account key. You can scope a SAS to a specific container, specify allowed operations (read only), set an expiry time (48 hours), and optionally restrict to an IP range. After expiry, the token becomes invalid. Sharing the account key would give the partner full storage account access permanently and is a security risk. Anonymous blob access removes all authentication, making data publicly accessible to anyone.

questions.question: An organization needs blobs older than 90 days to automatically move to the Cool tier, and blobs older than 365 days to automatically move to the Archive tier. Which Azure Storage feature manages this automatically?
options: Azure Data Factory pipeline with a blob trigger
Azure Storage lifecycle management policy
Azure Blob versioning with retention policies
Azure Automation runbook with a daily schedule
questions.explanation: Azure Storage lifecycle management policies allow you to define rules that automatically transition blobs between access tiers or delete them based on age or last-modified date. Rules are defined in JSON and applied at the storage account or container level. For example: transition to Cool tier after 90 days since last modification, transition to Archive after 365 days. Policies run daily at no additional cost. This is the native, purpose-built feature for automated tiering. Automation runbooks and Data Factory could achieve this but add operational complexity.

questions.question: An Azure Monitor metric alert fires when a VM scale set's average CPU exceeds 85% for 5 minutes. The team needs the alert to also (a) email two on-call DLs, (b) post to a webhook, (c) run a Logic App. Where is the email + webhook + Logic App configured — separately from the alert condition?
options: In the alert rule's condition settings page — sets metric/threshold, not the email/webhook/logic-app delivery channel
In an Action Group associated with the alert rule — defines email, webhook, and Logic App destinations attached to one or many alerts
In Azure Monitor diagnostic settings — routes raw logs, doesn't deliver alerts via email/webhook/logic app
In the scale-set's autoscale rule — scales the resource, no email/webhook/logic-app delivery
questions.explanation: In Azure Monitor, alert rules define when to fire an alert (condition, threshold, evaluation window), while Action Groups define what happens when an alert fires. An Action Group contains one or more action types: email/SMS notifications, Azure Function, Logic App, Automation Runbook, webhook, ITSM connector, and more. Multiple alert rules can share the same Action Group. This separation of concerns allows you to reuse notification configurations across many alert rules and modify notification recipients without changing alert conditions.

questions.question: An admin wants a shared, persistent, drag-and-drop visual surface in the Azure portal that combines (a) Log Analytics KQL query tiles, (b) Azure Monitor metric charts, (c) resource health tiles for selected resources. The artefact should be portal-resident and pinnable, not a workbook with parameter-driven interactivity. Which artefact?
options: Azure Monitor Alerts summary blade — list of alerts, not a customisable dashboard
Azure Monitor Workbooks — interactive parameterised reports, different artefact than a portal dashboard
Azure Dashboard (shared portal dashboard) — the drag-and-drop pinnable surface in the portal
Log Analytics workspace overview blade — workspace-scoped overview, not a cross-resource dashboard
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Workbooks provide a flexible canvas for combining multiple data types: KQL log queries, metric charts, resource health, text, links, and parameters. Workbooks are interactive (parameters drive queries dynamically) and can be shared across the organization. They are ideal for creating custom operational runbooks, incident reports, and application health dashboards. Azure Portal shared dashboards can include metric charts but lack the KQL query and interactive parameter capabilities of Workbooks. Workbooks are available within both Azure Monitor and resource blades.

questions.question: A company applies Azure Policy to enforce that all resources in a subscription must have a 'CostCenter' tag. A new storage account is deployed without this tag. What Azure Policy effect would automatically add the missing tag with a default value rather than blocking or flagging the deployment?
options: The Audit effect
The Deny effect
The Modify effect
The DeployIfNotExists effect
questions.explanation: The Modify effect in Azure Policy adds, updates, or removes tags on resources during creation or update operations. Unlike Deny (which blocks deployments missing the tag) or Audit (which only flags non-compliance), Modify actively alters the resource's properties to bring it into compliance. A Modify policy can add a 'CostCenter' tag with a default value when one is not provided. The policy requires a managed identity with Contributor rights to make modifications. DeployIfNotExists is used to deploy additional resources, not to modify tags on the deployed resource itself.

questions.question: An enterprise has dozens of subscriptions under nested management groups. The CISO requires a policy that EVERY existing subscription AND every future subscription must inherit, with a SINGLE assignment to maintain. Which scope satisfies the requirement?
options: Assign the policy to each subscription individually — does not include future subscriptions automatically; multiple assignments to manage
Assign the policy at the Root (Tenant) Management Group level — single assignment, all current AND future subscriptions inherit it via management-group hierarchy
Assign the policy at each resource group scope — wrong scope, no subscription-level future inheritance
Configure the rule in Microsoft Defender for Cloud — its own management UI, NOT an Azure Policy assignment
questions.explanation: Azure Policy assignments inherit DOWNWARD through the management-group hierarchy. Assigning at the Tenant Root MG means every subscription — current and future — receives the policy automatically. Per-subscription assignment doesn't auto-include new subscriptions. Defender enforces its OWN recommendations, not arbitrary policies. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A company wants to enforce a standard Azure environment for new projects that includes specific RBAC assignments, resource groups in approved locations, and required Azure Policy assignments — all deployed together as a single versioned package. Which Azure governance tool supports this pattern?
options: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates
Azure Blueprints versioned packages
Azure Policy initiative definitions
Terraform modules with shared state
questions.explanation: Azure Blueprints allow you to define a repeatable set of Azure resources that implements and enforces organizational standards. A blueprint can contain artifacts including: RBAC role assignments, Azure Policy definitions/assignments, ARM templates, and resource groups. Blueprints are versioned and can be assigned to subscriptions, with assignment tracked for compliance. Unlike ARM templates (which deploy resources but do not enforce ongoing compliance) or Policy (which enforces rules but does not deploy infrastructure), Blueprints combine both governance enforcement and infrastructure deployment.

questions.question: A finance team notices their Azure spending is close to the monthly budget. They want to receive an email notification when spending reaches 80% of the budget, and another when it reaches 100%. Which Azure Cost Management feature enables these notifications?
options: Azure Monitor metric alerts on the subscription cost metric
Azure Cost Management budgets with alert thresholds
Azure Advisor cost optimization recommendations
Azure Policy with a cost audit effect on resources
questions.explanation: Azure Cost Management budgets allow you to set spending thresholds and configure alert notifications at specific percentage thresholds (e.g., 80% and 100%). Alert recipients can be configured as email addresses or Action Groups. Budgets can be scoped to subscriptions, resource groups, or management groups, and can track actual costs or forecasted costs. Azure Monitor does not natively alert on subscription cost as a standard metric. Azure Advisor provides cost optimization recommendations but does not send budget threshold alerts.

questions.question: A development team builds container images as part of a CI/CD pipeline and wants to store them in a private registry in Azure that integrates natively with AKS for pulling images without managing registry credentials manually on each node. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure Blob Storage container with Docker layer caching enabled
Docker Hub private repository with Azure AD integration enabled
Azure Container Registry (ACR) with AKS managed identity attached
Azure Container Apps with the built-in image registry feature
questions.explanation: Azure Container Registry (ACR) is Azure's managed Docker and OCI registry. When AKS is configured to use an ACR by attaching it (az aks update --attach-acr), AKS nodes receive the AcrPull role via the cluster's managed identity, allowing Kubernetes to pull images from ACR without storing registry credentials as Kubernetes secrets. This is the native, recommended integration. Docker Hub is an external service with rate limits and requires separate credential management. ACR also supports geo-replication, content trust, and vulnerability scanning.

questions.question: A DevOps team needs to automatically build a new container image in Azure Container Registry whenever code is pushed to their GitHub repository, without setting up external CI/CD infrastructure. Which ACR feature provides this capability?
options: ACR Tasks with a source code trigger
AKS continuous deployment with Flux GitOps
Azure DevOps pipeline with ACR push action
ACR geo-replication with webhook triggers
questions.explanation: ACR Tasks is a suite of features within Azure Container Registry that automates container image builds and maintenance. A 'quick task' builds images on demand; a task with a 'source code trigger' automatically builds a new image when code is committed to a connected GitHub, Azure Repos, or Bitbucket repository (via webhook). Tasks can also trigger on base image updates. This eliminates the need for a separate CI server just for building and pushing container images. ACR Tasks run in Azure on managed compute, not on your own infrastructure.

questions.question: A company backs up Azure VMs using a Recovery Services vault with a backup policy that runs daily. Due to a ransomware attack, all VM disks have been encrypted by malware. The team needs to restore a VM from a backup taken 3 days ago to a different region for immediate investigation. Which Recovery Services vault feature supports this?
options: Instant Restore from a recovery point snapshot in the same region
Cross-Region Restore using the paired-region copy of the vault data
File-level recovery to mount the disk from 3 days ago for inspection
Azure Site Recovery failover into the paired secondary region
questions.explanation: Cross-Region Restore (CRR) allows you to restore Azure VMs to the secondary (paired) region using backup data replicated to that region by the Recovery Services vault (when geo-redundant storage is configured). This is useful for DR scenarios and investigations where the primary region is compromised or you need isolation. CRR must be enabled on the vault in advance. Instant Restore provides fast recovery using local snapshots but only in the same region. ASR is for live replication and failover, not for restoring from backup snapshots.

questions.question: An Azure VM backup policy needs to meet the following requirements: daily backups retained for 30 days, weekly backups (Sunday) retained for 12 weeks, and monthly backups retained for 12 months. Which backup policy type and tier supports all of these retention rules in a single policy?
options: Standard backup policy with the Enhanced tier subtype
Enhanced backup policy with Vault-Standard tier subtype
Standard backup policy with daily recovery points only
Custom backup policy created via Azure Backup Center
questions.explanation: Azure VM backup supports Enhanced policies (also called policy sub-type 'Enhanced') that are required for features like multiple daily backups and tiering. However, for the specific combination of daily/weekly/monthly retention tiers in a single policy, the Standard backup policy already supports GFS (Grandfather-Father-Son) retention with daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention points. The Enhanced policy additionally supports hourly backups and tiering to Vault-Archive for long-term retention cost savings. For this scenario, a standard policy with GFS retention rules covers all three retention requirements.

questions.question: An Azure Firewall is deployed in a hub VNet to inspect all traffic between spoke VNets and the internet. However, VMs in the spoke VNets are still bypassing the firewall and routing directly to the internet. What configuration is missing?
options: An NSG on the Azure Firewall subnet blocking direct internet egress from the spokes
A UDR for 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at the Azure Firewall private IP, attached to each spoke
A VNet peering between the hub and spoke VNets with gateway transit enabled
An Application Rule collection in the Azure Firewall allowing internet traffic out
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall sits in the hub VNet but VMs in spoke VNets use Azure's default system routes, which route 0.0.0.0/0 directly to the internet gateway. To force traffic through Azure Firewall, you must create a User Defined Route (UDR) with a 0.0.0.0/0 route and set the next hop to the Azure Firewall's private IP address. This route table must be associated with each spoke subnet that should have its traffic inspected. The VNet peering must already exist for connectivity, but without the UDR, traffic bypasses the firewall.

questions.question: An administrator needs to register authentication methods for Azure AD Multi-Factor Authentication. The organization requires the most phishing-resistant MFA method available in Azure AD. Which authentication method should be prioritized?
options: SMS one-time passcode sent to a registered mobile phone
Microsoft Authenticator app push notifications and TOTP
FIDO2 hardware security keys (such as YubiKey)
Voice call approval to a registered phone number
questions.explanation: FIDO2 security keys (hardware keys like YubiKey) provide the strongest phishing resistance of all MFA methods available in Azure AD. They use public-key cryptography bound to the specific origin (domain), so a phishing site on a different domain cannot capture or replay the credential. Microsoft Authenticator push notifications and TOTP codes are strong but can be compromised by real-time phishing proxy attacks (adversary-in-the-middle attacks). SMS is the weakest MFA method due to SIM swapping and SS7 vulnerabilities. FIDO2 is part of the passwordless authentication stack.

questions.question: An Azure VM running a critical application becomes unresponsive. The administrator cannot RDP or SSH into the VM, and Azure Bastion also fails to connect. The boot diagnostics show the VM is stuck at a 'Applying computer settings' screen. Which Azure feature allows the administrator to view the VM's serial console output and send keyboard input without a network connection?
options: Azure Bastion Standard tier with ShareableLink
Azure VM Run Command extension feature
Azure Serial Console with Boot Diagnostics
Re-imaging the VM from a custom OS snapshot
questions.explanation: Azure Serial Console provides text-based console access to a VM through the VM's serial port (COM1), bypassing the network stack entirely. It works even when the OS is unresponsive at the network level, as long as the VM's hypervisor can communicate with the serial port. From the Serial Console, administrators can interrupt the boot process, run diagnostic commands, fix boot configuration, or access a rescue shell. It requires Boot Diagnostics to be enabled with a storage account or managed storage. The Run Command feature sends commands to the VM agent, which also requires the OS to be running properly.
